extracted.intended_audience: marketing researchers, academic grant reviewers, and advertising scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Summaries of A.A.A.A.-funded academic research projects on advertising, consumer information processing, and experimental methods, describing purposes, methods, findings, and methodological lessons for studying advertising effects and buyer behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility of consumer panel design
rubrics_metrics.description: The consumer panel design must be feasible for collecting a wide range of information about the purchase decision process and allow testing of complex decision models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel grants enabled researchers to confirm feasibility, partially test complex decision models, refine measures that serve as input into models, and expand the panel (e.g., into new geographic areas). The panel design's ability to support longitudinal, iterative measurement development is a key merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity of measurement instruments (attitudes and advertising exposure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measuring instruments must be sensitive enough to detect relationships between advertising exposure and attitudes toward tangible and intangible investments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of insensitive measures: advertising exposure measured merely as whether ads were noted can be almost universal for some assets, reducing variance and masking relationships. Instruments should be refined (e.g., beyond simple awareness) to increase sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to modify and add measures during panel studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel studies should permit modification of measures and addition of new measures during the study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This flexibility allows improvements in measurement sensitivity over time and contributes to test development methodology; it is an advantage of panel designs compared with fixed cross-sectional studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining and measuring advertising as an intangible asset
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing advertising's economic effects, advertising should be treated as an intangible asset and included in firm asset calculations and amortization schedules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to include intangible assets leads to biased estimates of rates of return. Correcting accounting (including advertising capital and amortization provisions) brings observed returns on advertising capital closer to returns on other capital types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating rates of amortization for advertising expenditures
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies estimating the annual rates of amortization for advertising in specific industries are required to value advertising as capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example industry estimates found 40–50% per annum for beer and 35–40% for cigarettes; automobile estimates were less reliable. Estimation methods should derive demand from firm-level demand functions aggregated to industry demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to analyzing advertising's influence on competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze advertising's competitive effects by modeling advertising as a joint-product (a 'service' supplementary to physical output) and examining market structure implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using this framework, the beer industry analysis found competitive conditions prevail despite heavy advertising; properly measuring capital can overturn conclusions that advertising reduces competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-phase framework for studying the advertising process
rubrics_metrics.description: A comprehensive research program should address (1) media choice/context, (2) internal mental processes of advertising perception, and (3) the nature/content of the advertising message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each phase has distinct methods: (1) media choice models using syndicated viewing data to predict program selection; (2) theory and structural equation testing linking stimulus → memory → comprehension → attitude → intention → behavior; (3) content analysis methodologies to define stimuli precisely in terms of attitudinal, comprehension, and intention components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media choice model criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Media choice models should predict individual TV program choice from relatively inexpensive aggregated viewing data and be usable to select program alternatives similar to 'ideal' preferences of market segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The model described is akin to voting models, can predict preferred program and preferred mix of programming, and may be refined by further segmentation or mathematical assumption adjustments; it outperformed simpler aggregate models in prediction accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise definition of advertising stimuli for causal inference
rubrics_metrics.description: To attribute effects to advertising, the stimulus must be defined precisely in terms of content components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content analysis of TV, magazine, and newspaper ads should parse attitudinal, comprehension, and intention components; without precise stimulus definition, observed effects may be confounded with other stimuli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of panel data plus structural equations to estimate causal pathways
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical testing should estimate equations linking advertising recall → brand comprehension → brand attitude → intention → actual purchase, solving by computer to obtain relative strength estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel data and simultaneous equation methods can provide estimates of influence strengths and relationships among influences; results inform which links are strongest under stable conditions and guide managerial recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-controlled experimental technique: usability and efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: A computer-controlled experimental method should allow non-technical experimenters to design sophisticated communications experiments quickly and with minimal technical skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The technique requires only rudimentary typing skills and a clear problem conception; it automates presentation of stimuli, response capture, storage, and statistical analysis, reducing coding burden and speeding replication across geographical areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-controlled experimentation: reliability, replicability, and validity considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer-controlled experiments should demonstrate stable results across replications and consistency with traditional methods, while field validation is needed for external validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: greater experimental control, fast replication, and consistency with traditional communications experiments. Limitations: some lack of realism may impair external generalizability and further field testing is required before definitive validity claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off between experimental realism and control
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers must balance realism and experimental control: lower realism can allow stronger statistical relationships and refinement, while higher realism is needed for generalizability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In exploratory stages, high control and some artificiality may be advantageous for identifying promising strategies; promising alternatives should later be tested in field settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of response time as an unobtrusive measure of message favorability
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure rapidity of response (using computer clocks) as an indicator of message favorability: favorable messages elicit faster responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings showed favorable messages processed most rapidly and neutral messages slowest, suggesting response time may serve as an unobtrusive proxy for message favorability in message analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include personality variables and brand loyalty in models of information processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Models of advertising effectiveness should incorporate personality traits (e.g., risk-taking propensity) and brand loyalty because they influence how individuals process information and thus affect purchase choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personality variables tend to relate indirectly to brand choice by affecting information processing style; brand loyalty biases perception of persuasive communications and should be accounted for in models and campaign design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychometric testing of empathic skills for communication professionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Test professional advertising communicators for empathic skills (two types: sensitivity to individual differences and sensitivity to the generalized other) using validated instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empathic skills definitions drawn from Hulett and Bronfenbrenner; Type I tests (interpersonal sensitivity) used Guilford-developed instruments; Type II (stereotypic understanding) used 'Judgment of Interests' test. Hypothesis testing compared agency samples with college and high-school samples using standard significance thresholds (e.g., .001, .05).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of established instruments and comparison samples for validation
rubrics_metrics.description: When testing skills (e.g., empathy), use established psychometric instruments with known comparison means and include multiple comparison groups (college students, high school students, psychology samples) to evaluate significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: agency professionals' combined Guilford scores and JI scores were compared with normative samples and showed significant differences; one sub-sample (account personnel) outperformed a psychology sample on the Type II test.
